item.title: Higher Rates Hit the Fiscal Side, Not the Private Sector
item.content:encoded:
November 16, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

Corporate America and households both locked in low rates during the pandemic, with firms refinancing their debt and homeowners securing record-low mortgages.

Washington didn’t, and its interest bill has more than doubled from about $500 billion in summer 2020 to about $1.25 trillion today, so the economy is now far more sensitive to rates through the government than through the private sector, see charts below.

The bottom line is that the cost of higher rates has landed on the fiscal side rather than on companies and consumers, which is why the tightening cycle has done so little to slow the private economy.

item.title: Strong Growth, Rising Prices and a Fed Behind the Curve
item.content:encoded:
November 14, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

October nonfarm payrolls and CPI were strong, the AI spending boom continues and the Atlanta Fed estimates fourth-quarter GDP growth at 3.5%, significantly above the 2% potential growth rate.

At the same time, regional Fed surveys of prices paid, shifted six months forward, point to a continued strong uptrend in inflation, with PCE inflation moving towards 6%, see chart below.

The bottom line is that strong demand, combined with ongoing supply shocks to imports, labor and energy, raises the risk that the Fed is falling behind the curve and will have to raise rates much more than markets currently expect.

item.title: Europe’s Defense Boom Is Reaching Beyond Defense Companies
item.content:encoded:
November 13, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

European defense spending grew 16% last year and is expected to grow at double-digit rates for the next three years, see chart below.

NATO members have committed to spend 3.5% of GDP on core defense and another 1.5% on broader security, although fiscal constraints will influence how quickly countries get there.

Recent disruptions, from attacks on subsea cables to drones near airports, to supermarket fridges and outages affecting critical infrastructure, may bring forward the need for that broader 1.5% security spending.

But where this spending goes is also broadening beyond traditional weapons and defense technology. Spending increasingly includes cybersecurity, critical infrastructure, maritime and pipeline sensors, resilient energy systems, as well as the local industrial capacity needed to manufacture and secure resilient supply chains. Many of these businesses serve both commercial and national-security markets.

The bottom line is that some of the next beneficiaries of Europe's defense buildout may sit in infrastructure, energy and industrial technology rather than in the defense sector itself.

Written by Huw van Steenis

This broad-based strength in consumer spending is in sharp contrast to the ongoing decline in consumer confidence across the income distribution, see the second chart.

The bottom line is that there is a significant difference between what consumers are saying and what they are actually doing.

item.title: Utilities, Defense and Digitization are Driving Europe’s Capex Revival
item.content:encoded:
November 10, 2026

About the Author Torsten Slok

Partner, Chief Economist

Share

European companies are investing again. The capex-to-sales ratio is approaching a 10-year high, and European listed companies are expected to spend €77 billion more on capex in 2028 than in 2025, see charts below.

Utilities alone account for €31 billion, or around 40%, of the increase. Defense capex is expected to rise 36%, industrials excluding defense 24% and information technology 78%.

This comes after a long period of underinvestment. Across Europe, higher spending on energy, grids, defense, reshoring, infrastructure and digitalization is now lifting capital intensity.

The US capex cycle is dominated by AI. Europe's has a different mix: more of the increase is being driven by infrastructure, defense and power.

The bottom line is that capex is rebounding across Europe, and the industrial renaissance has gone global.

Written by Huw van Steenis
